docs.title: kigit
docs.text:
kigit utilizes the use of git logs in order to allow user to perform diffs between their pcb and schematic files. It provides a proper visual feedback which helps in identifying changes made per commit basis. Hence where its name came from, combination of Ki from KiCAD and git itself (kigit!).

What it can do:

  • Compare your PCB between any two commits, visually
  • Show what changed on your symbols and their fields
  • Show your buses and where they're routed
  • Work without git too: just point it at two folders (see Without Git)

Have a look at the demo below to get a feel for it.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• PCB Viewer

    Hover a trace to highlight its net. Added copper in green, removed in red, moved in blue, with each net's length change.

  • Schematic Viewer

    Every sheet drawn with the same colours: parts whose value, footprint or connections changed, and pins that joined or left a net.

  • Source Panel

    The changed lines of the KiCad files, old and new side by side, for whatever you hover.

  • GUI

    Open a project, pick two commits from its history and compare. No command line needed.

docs.title: What kigit is not
docs.text:
kigit is an application that was built out of frustration of not having a kind of proper "git diff" for kicad for myself. Having came from a software background and being used to utilizing git versioning for all of my projects, not being able to do the same in a manner that I can compare my pcb and schematic visually between different commits without having to diff the .kicad_pcb and .kicad_sch files really frustates me. I am aware of the fact that there are other resources out there as shown below:

  • KiRI
  • KiCAD-Prism
  • KiHub

They all have their pros and cons. KiRI is what got me excited about diffing schematics in the first place, and honestly, huge respect to the folks behind it. It's a great community effort, built well before AI was a thing.

The other two I didn't even know existed when I started. Funnily enough, not even Claude mentioned them when I first went looking for alternatives.

KiCAD-Prism and KiHub are in the same space and cover a lot of what kigit does. KiCAD-Prism is a whole package: free, open source, and the demos look amazing. But it needs a fair bit of Docker setup, which can be a turn-off if you're a hobbyist who just wants to design boards. KiHub needs a login, doesn't run offline, and is really aimed at teams collaborating (PR reviews and that kind of thing).

Me? I'm a hobbyist who only recently got into PCB design and out of this frustration, I figured: why not just make my own PCB diff that does just enough for what I need? Nothing fancy. It runs locally, it's a simple download, and it works on Linux and Windows. (Sorry macOS folks, I'm broke and not about to buy a Mac just for this.)

So, what kigit is not is a collaboration tool. It's for people who wants a simple app they can download, or open in a browser, to check what changed in their PCB designs. That's it.

Disclaimer

When I say "I built it", it was mostly my best mate, Claude.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
cd path/to/my-board        # a KiCad project in a git repository
kigit HEAD~1               # the last commit vs your working tree
kigit gui                  # or pick commits in the GUI

See Installation to get kigit, and Overview for how it works.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page is for anyone who wants to read or change kigit's code. It explains how the pieces fit together and where to find things. It doesn't go into every function: for that, the headers in include/ are short and commented.

docs.title: Bird's-eye view
docs.text:
kigit takes two versions of a KiCad project, works out what changed, and writes one HTML page that shows it.

It's built from four parts:

Part Language What it does Core (kigit_core) C++20 Reads, parses, matches and diffs the files, and builds the data for the page Command line (kigit) C++20 Parses options, runs the core, prints the summary, writes the page Viewer (resources/) HTML + JS Draws the board and schematic in the browser from that data GUI (gui/) Python (NiceGUI) A front end that calls the kigit command line

The core never draws anything, and the viewer never reads KiCad files. They only meet through JSON.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Every comparison runs the same steps:

flowchart TD
    subgraph UI["① User interaction"]
        direction LR
        GUI["GUI (NiceGUI)<br/>open a project, pick two commits"] -->|runs| CLI["kigit command<br/>kigit A..B"]
    end

    subgraph BE["② Backend: kigit (C++)"]
        direction LR
        R["Read<br/>git show / files"] --> P["Parse<br/>s-expressions"]
        P --> M["Model<br/>Board + Schematic"]
        M --> D["Diff<br/>match old vs new"]
        D --> RP["Report<br/>JSON → HTML"]
    end

    subgraph FE["③ Frontend: viewer (browser)"]
        direction LR
        V["viewer.html<br/>embedded JSON"] --> PCB["PCB tab<br/>pcb.js"]
        V --> SCH["Schematic tab<br/>sch.js"]
        V --> SRC["Source panel<br/>source.js"]
    end

    UI -->|two revisions| BE
    BE -->|one HTML file| FE

The backend also prints a summary to the terminal straight from the diff, and the GUI shows the finished page in its own window. In the viewer, hovering, pinning and zooming all happen in the browser: nothing goes back to the backend.

Layer What it is Where ① User interaction How you ask for a comparison: a kigit command, or the GUI, which runs that same command for you src/commands/, gui/ ② Backend Everything that touches KiCad files: read, parse, model, diff, and write the page. Never draws anything src/git/, src/utils/, src/pcb/, src/sch/, src/report/ ③ Frontend The page in the browser: draws the board and schematic from the JSON and handles hover, pinning and zoom. Never reads KiCad files resources/

The backend's steps in more detail:

Step What happens Where 1. Read git show <rev>:<path> for the board and every schematic sheet, or the file on disk for LOCAL / --files. If the board moved in history, it finds the most similar board in that revision. git/git.cpp, git/locate.cpp 2. Parse The text becomes a tree of Nodes (lists and atoms). The parser knows nothing about KiCad; it also records each list's byte span in the file. utils/sexpr.cpp 3. Model The tree becomes KiCad things: a Board (tracks, arcs, vias, pads, footprints, zones) and a Schematic (sheets, symbols, wires, labels, buses), whose nets kigit works out itself. pcb/board.cpp, sch/schematic.cpp 4. Diff Old and new are matched (by KiCad ID, then by geometry) and every item gets a status. Totals are summed per net. pcb/diff.cpp, sch/sch_diff.cpp 5. Report The diff becomes JSON for the viewer, plus the old and new text of changed items with --source. report/html.cpp, report/source.cpp 6. Page The JSON is put into the viewer template, which is compiled into the binary, and written as one file. report/html.cpp (render_html) 7. Draw The browser runs the page's JS, which draws SVG from the JSON. resources/*.js

The terminal summary (the nets table, the schematic changes) is printed from the diff in step 4, not from the JSON. With --json, steps 6 and 7 are skipped and the JSON is written instead.

The node trees and how they become Board and Schematic are shown in detail under From nodes to structs.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
The parser only knows two shapes of node, and every KiCad file is built from them:

Shape Looks like In Node List (width 0.25), (segment ...) is_list = true; name() is its first atom ("width"), children holds the rest Atom width, 0.25, "F.Cu" atom holds the text; quoted = true if it was written in quotes

So (layer "F.Cu") is a list named layer with one quoted atom, and node.arg(0) returns F.Cu. Lists also carry their span, so the source panel can show the exact lines later.

docs.title: From nodes to structs
docs.text:
The KiCad meaning comes in step 3, where each kind of list is turned into a field of Board or Schematic:

.kicad_pcb → Board.kicad_sch → Schematic 
flowchart LR
    P0["(kicad_pcb)"]
    P0 --> P1["(segment)"]
    P0 --> P2["(arc)"]
    P0 --> P3["(via)"]
    P0 --> P4["(footprint)"]
    P4 --> P5["(pad)"]
    P4 --> P6["(property)"]
    P4 --> P7["(fp_line) (fp_arc) (fp_rect)<br/>(fp_circle) (fp_poly) (fp_text)"]
    P0 --> P8["(zone)"]
    P8 --> P9["(polygon)"]
    P8 --> P10["(filled_polygon)"]
    P0 --> P11["(gr_line) (gr_arc) (gr_rect)<br/>(gr_circle) (gr_poly) (gr_text)"]
    P0 --> P12["(net)"]

    P1 -.-> I["items"]
    P2 -.-> I
    P3 -.-> I
    P5 -.-> I
    P4 -.-> FP["footprints"]
    P6 -.-> FP
    P7 -.-> SK["silk<br/>(--silkscreen)"]
    P9 -.-> Z["zones"]
    P10 -.-> X["skipped"]
    P11 -.-> O["outline<br/>(Edge.Cuts)"]
    P11 -.-> SK
    P12 -.-> N["net names"]

    classDef field fill:#7e57c2,stroke:#7e57c2,color:#fff
    classDef skip stroke-dasharray:4 3
    class I,FP,SK,Z,O,N field
    class X skip

Solid lines are the file's nesting; dotted lines show which Board field each node ends up in.

Node Becomes Notes (segment) items, kind Track (arc) items, kind Arc (via) items, kind Via (pad) inside (footprint) items, kind Pad Position made absolute from the footprint's (at) (footprint) footprints Reference and value from its (property) lists; its fp_* graphics are compared too (zone) zones Its (filled_polygon) lists are skipped: KiCad recomputes them on every refill (gr_*) on Edge.Cuts outline The board shape (gr_*) / (fp_*) on silkscreen silk Only with --silkscreen (net) Net names Older files list nets by number at the top 
flowchart LR
    S0["(kicad_sch)"]
    S0 --> S1["(lib_symbols)"]
    S1 --> S2["(symbol)<br/>part definition"]
    S0 --> S3["(symbol)<br/>placed part"]
    S0 --> S4["(wire)"]
    S0 --> S5["(junction)<br/>(no_connect)"]
    S0 --> S6["(label) (global_label)<br/>(hierarchical_label)"]
    S0 --> S7["(bus) (bus_entry)<br/>(bus_alias)"]
    S0 --> S8["(sheet)"]
    S8 --> S9["(pin)"]
    S0 --> S10["(text)"]
    S0 --> S11["(polyline) (rectangle)<br/>(circle) (arc) (bezier)"]

    S2 -.-> D["defs"]
    S3 -.-> SY["symbols"]
    S4 -.-> W["wires"]
    S5 -.-> J["junctions<br/>no_connects"]
    S6 -.-> L["labels"]
    S9 -.-> L
    S7 -.-> B["buses, bus_entries<br/>bus_aliases"]
    S8 -.-> SB["sheet_boxes<br/>+ child sheet loaded"]
    S10 -.-> T["texts"]
    S11 -.-> DR["drawings"]

    classDef field fill:#7e57c2,stroke:#7e57c2,color:#fff
    class D,SY,W,J,L,B,SB,T,DR field

Solid lines are the file's nesting; dotted lines show which Schematic field each node ends up in.

Node Becomes Notes (lib_symbols) → (symbol) defs Each part type's pins and drawing, stored in the file (symbol) symbols A placed part. Power symbols (+3.3V, GND) are symbols too (wire) wires (junction), (no_connect) junctions, no_connects (label), (global_label), (hierarchical_label) labels Their names join nets across wires and sheets (bus), (bus_entry), (bus_alias) buses, bus_entries, bus_aliases (sheet) sheet_boxes, and its file is loaded as a new sheet Through the FileReader (pin) inside (sheet) labels, kind SheetPin Connects the parent sheet to the child's hierarchical labels (text) texts (polyline), (rectangle), (circle), (arc), (bezier) drawings Drawn only; they don't connect anything

After every sheet is loaded, kigit works out nets from the wires, labels, pins and buses.

docs.title: Code map
docs.text: Headers live in include/<dir>/, and their sources in src/<dir>/ with the same names.

docs.title: utils/
docs.text:
The building blocks with no KiCad knowledge.

  • sexpr: the s-expression parser. sexpr::parse(text) returns a Node tree, with each list's span (where it starts and ends in the text).
  • platform: everything that differs between Windows and Linux: running programs, finding them on PATH, opening a browser, home and state folders.
  • log: the session log (spdlog), one file per run.

docs.title: git/
docs.text:
• git: a thin wrapper around the git command line: resolve a revision, show a file at a revision, log, list files. kigit runs the real git program rather than a library, so it behaves exactly like the user's git.
  • locate: finding the board in a revision when it was moved or renamed (find_similar_board), by comparing footprints and nets.

docs.title: pcb/
docs.text:
• board: load_board(text) turns a .kicad_pcb into a Board. Tracks, arcs, vias and pads are all one Item type with a kind, because the diff treats them the same way.
  • diff: diff_boards(old, new) matches items and footprints and returns a Diff: each item with its status, plus per-net and per-footprint totals.

docs.title: sch/
docs.text:
• schematic: load_schematic(root_file, reader) loads a schematic and all its sheets, then works out the nets: which pins each wire, label, power symbol and bus connects. It reads sheets through a FileReader function, not from disk, so the same code works for a git revision, the working tree, or a folder.
  • sch_diff: diff_schematics(old, new) matches parts (by KiCad ID, then reference) and nets (by label, then shared pins), and sorts each change into electrical, fields only or cosmetic.
  • netcheck: --check-netlist, which compares kigit's nets with a netlist exported by KiCad. This is how the net logic is tested against KiCad itself.

docs.title: report/
docs.text:
• html: turns boards, schematics and diffs into the viewer's JSON (report_data, schematic_view_json), and render_html puts that JSON into the page template.
  • source: the text snippets for the source panel. SourceFile turns a Span into whole lines with line numbers; SourceTable collects one entry per changed item.

docs.title: commands/
docs.text:
The command line, one file per command, in namespace kigit::cmd. Only the kigit executable has these; they aren't part of kigit_core.

File Command options Parsing the command line and --help diff The main job: steps 1 to 6 above, plus --check-netlist summary The tables printed to the terminal history --log: the commit list for the GUI projects --projects: KiCad projects in a folder, for the GUI gui kigit gui: finds uv and starts the Python app common Helpers they share, like finding the project folder

src/main.cpp starts the log, then picks the command.

docs.title: resources/ (the viewer)
docs.text:
File What it does viewer.html The page shell: layout, styles, and slots for the data and scripts pcb.js The PCB tab: drawing, hover, pinning, the net list sch.js The schematic tab: sheets, parts, wires, nets source.js The source panel: the side-by-side text diff (line diff done in JS) shell.js The tabs and everything shared between them

At build time, CMake puts the four scripts into viewer.html and compiles the result into the binary as a byte array. At run time, render_html replaces the /*KIGIT_DATA*/ slot with the JSON. That's why the output is a single file with no dependencies.

docs.title: gui/
docs.text:
A NiceGUI app (gui/kigit_gui/). It doesn't link to the core: it runs the kigit command line (kigit.py) and uses its JSON output (--projects, --log, --json) or its page (-o -).

  • app.py: the screens (open a project, pick commits, compare).
  • kigit.py: calling the kigit binary.
  • folder_picker.py, logs.py: the folder dialog and the log view.

kigit gui starts it with uv, which sets up the Python environment on first run.

docs.title: Rules that hold everywhere
docs.text:
These are worth keeping when you change things.

  • The core doesn't draw, and the viewer doesn't parse. All drawing is in resources/*.js; all KiCad file reading is in C++. They only share JSON.
  • The parser knows nothing about KiCad. sexpr returns lists and atoms. Meaning (what a segment is) belongs in pcb/ and sch/.
  • OS-specific code lives in utils/platform only. Everything else is plain C++ and builds the same on Windows and Linux.
  • git is only used through git/. Nothing else runs git.
  • Schematics are read through a FileReader. That keeps the loader independent of where the files come from.
  • stdout stays clean. With -o - the page or JSON goes to stdout, so messages go to stderr or the log.
  • The page is one self-contained file. No server, no external scripts. It must open from disk, years later.
  • Big extras are opt-in. Silkscreen (--silkscreen) and the source panel (--source) make pages bigger, so they're off by default.

docs.title: Build and dependencies
docs.text:
• CMake builds kigit_core (a static library with everything except the command line) and the kigit executable. Tests link kigit_core directly.
  • Libraries are git submodules in submodules/: nlohmann_json (JSON), spdlog (logging), doctest (tests).
  • CI (GitHub Actions) builds and tests on Windows (MSVC) and Linux (GCC) on every push. Tagged releases build the Windows installer, the Windows zip and the Linux tarball.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: You want to... Look at Support a new KiCad item on the board pcb/board.cpp (load it), pcb/diff.cpp (match it), report/html.cpp (send it), resources/pcb.js (draw it) Change how items are matched pcb/diff.cpp or sch/sch_diff.cpp Fix a schematic net that's wrong sch/schematic.cpp, and test it with --check-netlist against KiCad's netlist Change what the terminal prints commands/summary.cpp Add a command-line option commands/options.cpp, then use it in the command Change the look of the viewer resources/viewer.html (styles) and the matching .js file Change the GUI gui/kigit_gui/app.py

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• git on your PATH (Git for Windows on Windows)
  • Windows 10/11 or Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+, Fedora 36+ or similar)

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Download kigit-<version>-setup.exe from the Releases page.
  2. Run it. No admin rights are needed.

It adds kigit to your PATH and a kigit entry to the Start menu that opens the GUI.

Warning

The first kigit gui takes about a minute, since it grabs Python and the GUI's packages. After that, it's instant. (The command line doesn't need any of that, so it's quick from the start.)

Portable

The Releases page also has a zip. Unzip it anywhere and run bin\kigit.exe.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Download kigit-<version>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz from the Releases page and unpack it into ~/.local:

tar -xzf kigit-*-linux-x86_64.tar.gz -C ~/.local --strip-components=1
kigit --version    # ~/.local/bin must be on your PATH (it is on most distros)
kigit --help # Shows all optional commands and some example
kigit gui # Launches the GUI for kigit

It brings its own copy of uv for the GUI (in ~/.local/libexec/kigit), so a uv you already have isn't touched.

To uninstall:

rm ~/.local/bin/kigit
rm -r ~/.local/share/kigit ~/.local/libexec/kigit
rm -r ~/.local/state/kigit    # optional: the GUI's Python environment and the logs

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
Needs a C++20 compiler and CMake 3.16+. The libraries (nlohmann_json, spdlog, doctest) are git submodules:

git clone --recursive https://github.com/KhalidOwlWalid/kigit.git
cd kigit
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build -j
cmake --install build --prefix ~/.local    # optional

On Windows, MSVC (Visual Studio 2022) and MinGW-w64 GCC 11+ both work:

cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --config Release
build\Release\kigit.exe gui

The GUI also needs uv on your PATH when built from source.

docs.title: What is kigit?
docs.text:
kigit is a visual diff for KiCad projects kept in git. Text diffs of .kicad_pcb and .kicad_sch files are thousands of lines of coordinates. kigit turns them into a picture of the board and schematic where every change is coloured, so you can review a layout change the way you'd review code.

It is a single command-line program (C++) plus an optional GUI. It runs on Windows and Linux.

It requires no internet connection, no logins, simply just an offline application that you can use to review your PCB changes.

docs.title: kigit CLI
docs.text: kigit CLI provides you the ability to simply perform every action via the command line interface without the need for any GUI. As demonstrated in the video above, all functionalities are accessible from the cli, and it will generate the .html file which you can specify its output directory. If not provided, by default, it will be stored in kigit hidden directory .kigit/.

docs.title: kigit GUI
docs.text: Similar to kigit CLI, kigit GUI simply provides the you with the ability to do everything via GUI. This is much more desirable as it may be more intuitive and easy to perform comparison where needed.

docs.title: Two revisions
docs.text:
Every comparison is either between:

  • an old and a new revision
  • two commits (chosen by the unique hash found from the commits)
  • a commit and your uncommitted changes (LOCAL)
  • two folders when there's no git at all. "Added" always means added in the newer one.

docs.title: Matching
docs.text:
kigit matches items between the two revisions before colouring anything:

  • PCB: tracks, arcs, vias and pads are matched first by KiCad's internal ID, then by geometry (same kind, net, layers and coordinates to 1 nm). An item with the same ID and the same copper at a new place is moved, not removed and re-added, so moving a footprint doesn't light up the whole board.
  • Schematic: parts are matched by KiCad ID (then reference), so re-annotating shows as a rename. Nets are paired by label name, else by shared pins.

docs.title: What a change looks like in the actual kicad source file
docs.text:
Each example shows the same item in the old and new .kicad_pcb, side by side, the way the source panel shows it. Removed text is red, added text green, and the exact characters that changed are highlighted.

Track editedFootprint movedVia addedRedrawn, same copper

CHANGEDowl_v1.kicad_pcb:1204 → :12041204 (segment1204 (segment1205 (start 121.5 84.25)1205 (start 121.5 84.25)1206 (end 135 84.25)1206 (end 135 90.75)1207 (width 0.25)1207 (width 0.4)1208 (layer "F.Cu")1208 (layer "F.Cu")1209 (net 12)1209 (net 12)1210 (uuid "8c1f3e7a-52b4-4d0e-9a51-3c2f6d1b7e40")1210 (uuid "8c1f3e7a-52b4-4d0e-9a51-3c2f6d1b7e40")1211 )1211 )Same ID, but the copper itself changed (new end point and width). kigit draws the old track red and the new one green, and the net's length change is updated.

CHANGEDowl_v1.kicad_pcb:2310 → :23102310 (footprint "Resistor_SMD:R_0603_1608Metric"2310 (footprint "Resistor_SMD:R_0603_1608Metric"2311 (layer "F.Cu")2311 (layer "F.Cu")2312 (uuid "2b9d6c41-7f0a-4e83-b1d2-95c4a0e8f317")2312 (uuid "2b9d6c41-7f0a-4e83-b1d2-95c4a0e8f317")2313 (at 142.24 96.52 90)2313 (at 150.5 96.52 0)2314 (property "Reference" "R12"2314 (property "Reference" "R12"⋯ 31 unchanged lines2346 (pad "1" smd roundrect2346 (pad "1" smd roundrect2347 (at -0.825 0 90)2347 (at -0.825 0 90)2348 (size 0.8 0.95)2348 (size 0.8 0.95)2349 (layers "F.Cu" "F.Paste" "F.Mask")2349 (layers "F.Cu" "F.Paste" "F.Mask")Only the footprint's position and angle changed. Pad positions are stored relative to the footprint, so their text is the same, and the pads keep their IDs. kigit shows R12 and its pads as moved, not removed and re-added.

ADDED— → owl_v1.kicad_pcb:18761876 (via1877 (at 128.27 101.6)1878 (size 0.6)1879 (drill 0.3)1880 (layers "F.Cu" "B.Cu")1881 (net 3)1882 (uuid "e41a07c9-3d5b-48f2-a6e0-7b19c25d8a64")1883 )No item in the old file has this ID or this geometry, so the via is added: green, with nothing on the old side.

SAME COPPERowl_v1.kicad_pcb:1188 → :11881188 (segment1188 (segment1189 (start 98 72.5)1189 (start 98 72.5)1190 (end 110.25 72.5)1190 (end 110.25 72.5)1191 (width 0.25)1191 (width 0.25)1192 (layer "B.Cu")1192 (layer "B.Cu")1193 (net 7)1193 (net 7)1194 (uuid "5a0e93c2-18d4-4b6f-8e27-c3f1a9d04b85")1194 (uuid "f7c2d815-6e09-4a3b-b54d-0d8e2a61c9f3")1195 )1195 )You deleted the track and drew it again in exactly the same place, so KiCad gave it a new ID. The ID pass finds no match, but the geometry pass does (same kind, net, layer and coordinates), so kigit shows it as unchanged. A plain text diff would call this a change.

docs.title: Types of changes
docs.text:
Schematic changes are split into three types:

Type What counts Examples Electrical Anything that changes the circuit A part added or removed; its value, footprint or symbol changed; a pin moved to another net Fields only Text on a part that doesn't change the circuit BOM fields like MPN, or the reference Cosmetic Layout changes with the same connections Parts moved, wires redrawn, labels moved

docs.title: One HTML file
docs.text: The result is one self-contained HTML page with the PCB and schematic as tabs. It requires no server which you can open it, keep it, or attach it to a pull request.

docs.title: Further guidance
docs.text:
Follow the given order to see how kigit works from end-to-end:

  • Installing kigit
  • Using kigit Command Line (cli)
  • Using kigit GUI
  • General kigit User Interface (UI) Overview
  • Using PCB viewer
  • Using schematic viewer

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Custom-shaped pads are drawn as their anchor rectangle.
  • Footprint graphics (courtyards, fab) aren't drawn; silkscreen is optional.
  • Zones (copper pours) are drawn from the newer revision only and aren't diffed, because refilling a pour changes its shape every time.
  • Old KiCad 5 boards are parsed but less tested.
  • macOS isn't supported for now.

docs.title: Compare Two Commits
docs.text:
Review what the last commit changed on the board:

cd ~/boards/owl_v1
kigit HEAD~1..HEAD

kigit prints a summary and opens the page:

schematic: parts +1 -0, 8 changed electrically, 1 fields only, 0 only moved; 3 nets changed, 0 renamed, 1 only redrawn

Then:

  1. On the PCB tab, hover a green or red trace to see its whole net and how its length changed.
  2. Click to pin the net, and Esc to let go.
  3. Switch to the Schematic tab and hover an amber part to see what changed on it.

docs.title: Before you commit
docs.text:
Without a range, kigit compares HEAD with your working tree, so you can check your own changes before committing:

kigit

docs.title: With the file text
docs.text:
kigit --source HEAD~1..HEAD

adds the source panel: hover anything to see its lines in the old and new file.

docs.title: Moved or Renamed Boards
docs.text:
If the board isn't at the same path in one of the revisions (you moved hardware/owl.kicad_pcb to pcb/owl_v1.kicad_pcb, say), kigit searches that revision for every .kicad_pcb and picks the one sharing the most footprints and nets with the latest version of your board.

kigit 259cd18..HEAD

warning: pcb/owl_v1.kicad_pcb doesn't exist in 259cd18, using hardware/owl.kicad_pcb
         instead (98% match: 62 of 63 footprints and 74 of 74 nets are the same ...)
warning: the board was moved or renamed: hardware/owl.kicad_pcb (259cd18) -> pcb/owl_v1.kicad_pcb (f038da9)

The same warning shows in the viewer, and the comparison carries on.

Warning

If nothing is at least 25% similar, kigit stops and lists the boards it found instead of guessing.

The GUI follows the move too: the commit list includes the commits from before the folder was renamed.

docs.title: Without Git
docs.text:
Compare two copies of a board directly, e.g. two saved versions of the same project. No git repository needed; the older file goes first:

kigit --files owl_v1_old/owl_v1.kicad_pcb owl_v1/owl_v1.kicad_pcb
kigit old.kicad_pcb new.kicad_pcb              # two board files = --files

The schematic next to each board is compared too. The viewer labels the two sides by file name, or by folder name when both files have the same name.

docs.title: In the GUI
docs.text:
Press Compare folders in the header and pick each copy's folder. kigit finds the board in each (and the schematic next to it), and the viewer opens as usual.

Opening a project that isn't in git offers the same thing, with that project already filled in.

docs.title: Choosing revisions
docs.text:
kigit                      # HEAD vs the working tree
kigit HEAD~3               # HEAD~3 vs the working tree
kigit c46da63..HEAD        # two commits
kigit v1.0 v1.1 board.kicad_pcb

If you give the newer revision first, kigit swaps them so "added" always means "added in the newer revision".

docs.title: Choosing the project
docs.text:
Run it inside a project folder, or point at one from anywhere with --kicad-repo (short: -C):

kigit -C ~/boards/owl HEAD~1                 # finds the board in subfolders
kigit -C path/to/board.kicad_pro HEAD~1      # a .kicad_pro or .kicad_pcb works too

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
Option What it does -o FILE Write the page here (-o - for stdout) -n Don't open a browser -s, --stats Print every changed net (and cosmetic schematic changes) --json Write the data as JSON instead of the page --silkscreen Compare and draw silkscreen --source Add the source panel --files OLD NEW Compare two files, no git needed -V Print the log to the console, with debug lines --log-dir DIR, --no-log Where the log goes, or no log

Run kigit --help for the full list.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text:
What the GUI uses, if you want to build on it:

kigit --projects [--depth N]    # KiCad projects in the folder and below, as JSON
kigit --log [--max N] [--since DATE] [--until DATE] [--kicad-only]
                                # commits (+ uncommitted changes), as JSON
kigit -n -o - A..B              # the viewer page on stdout
kigit -n --json -o - A..B       # the data on stdout

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Every run keeps a log named after when it started:

Platform Default folder Linux ~/.local/state/kigit/log/ Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\kigit\log\

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
kigit gui                  # start in the current folder
kigit gui ~/path/to/board  # or any folder

On Windows the GUI opens in its own window (Edge WebView2, built into Windows 10/11); on Linux it opens in your web browser. --native and --browser choose; if a window can't be opened, it says why and uses the browser. It only listens on 127.0.0.1, so it isn't reachable from the network.

docs.title: 1. Open a project
docs.text: Type a folder or press Browse (folders holding KiCad files are marked). kigit looks for a project in that folder and up to two levels below. It tells you if it finds none, if the project has no .kicad_pcb, or if it isn't in a git repository; if it finds several, it asks which one.

docs.title: 2. Pick two commits
docs.text:
All commits are listed, newest first, tagged PCB / SCH when they changed the board or schematic. The top entry is your working tree: HEAD plus any uncommitted changes. Hover a message to read all of it.

  • Filter commits: how many to list, a date range, and "only commits that changed the board or schematic". If the project folder was renamed or moved, its history is followed through the old folders too.
  • Diff commits manually: type any two revisions git understands (hash, HEAD~3, branch, tag, or LOCAL), for when the commit you want isn't in the list.

docs.title: 3. Compare
docs.text: kigit diffs the two and the viewer opens on the schematic, with the PCB one tab away.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option What it does Include silkscreen Compare and draw F/B silkscreen (bigger pages) Include source Add the source panel (bigger pages) Compare folders Compare two copies of a project without git

Tip

The log button in the header shows the session's log file and its latest lines, handy for bug reports.

docs.title: PCB Viewer
docs.text:
The PCB tab draws both revisions of the board on top of each other.

Action What it does Hover a trace, via or pad Highlight its net, show the net's changes Click Pin the net (click again or Esc to clear) Scroll / drag Zoom / pan F Fit the board / Filter nets Double-click a net in the list Zoom to it

docs.title: How items are matched
docs.text:
Tracks, arcs, vias and pads are matched in two passes:

  1. By KiCad's ID (the ID KiCad gives every item and keeps when you move it; a pad uses its footprint's ID plus its pad number). Same ID and same place: unchanged. Same ID and same copper at a new place or angle: moved, shown in blue, with an optional ghost at the old position. Same ID but edited (a dragged track end, a new width or net): removed + added.
  2. By geometry for everything else: same kind, net, layers and coordinates (to 1 nm) means unchanged.

So moving a footprint or the whole layout shows as moved, not as everything removed and re-added, while re-routing still shows the new and old copper.

docs.title: Silkscreen
docs.text: Off by default (--silkscreen, or "Include silkscreen" in the GUI) since it makes pages bigger. Front silkscreen is drawn near-white, back purple and mirrored, each with its own layer toggle. Text uses a browser font, so it's close to KiCad's but not identical.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text: Copper pours are drawn from the newer revision only and aren't diffed, because refilling a pour changes its shape every time.

docs.title: Schematic Viewer
docs.text:
The Schematic tab draws each sheet (wires, parts, labels, sheet boxes) with the same colours as the PCB: green added, red dashed removed, amber for parts whose value, footprint or connections changed, grey unchanged.

Action What it does Hover a wire, label or pin Highlight its net; the tooltip shows pins that joined or left, renames, or "wiring redrawn, connections unchanged" Hover a part Its changes: fields (value, footprint, MPN...), pins moved to other nets, moved Click Pin it; the card can jump to other sheets the net is on Double-click a sheet box Open that sheet (Backspace goes back up) Sidebar Sheet tree with change counts, and the changes on the current sheet

"Old positions" shows moved parts' previous place as a faint ghost (off by default).

docs.title: Nets
docs.text:
kigit works out the schematic's nets itself, across all sheets, buses (D[0..7], groups, aliases like USB_C{USB}) and KiCad 10's multiple top-level sheets. You can check them against KiCad's own netlist:

kicad-cli sch export netlist -o owl.net owl_v1.kicad_sch
kigit --check-netlist owl.net

docs.title: In the terminal
docs.text:
Every run also prints the schematic changes:

schematic: parts +1 -0, 8 changed electrically, 1 fields only, 0 only moved; 3 nets changed, 0 renamed, 1 only redrawn
  ~ J3     J3.1 (Pin_1): /owl_v1/CAN Transceiver/CAN_H -> GND, moved
  + R19    R          [IOs] on +3.3V, GND
  ~ C14    Footprint Capacitor_SMD:C_0402_1005Metric -> Capacitor_SMD:C_0603_1608Metric
  ~ net GND                      joined: J3.1 (Pin_1), R19.2  left: J3.3 (Pin_3)

Note

The drawing is kigit's own, not KiCad's export: close to KiCad but with a different font, and images and text boxes aren't drawn yet.

docs.title: Source Panel
docs.text:
The source panel shows the text of what changed in the .kicad_pcb / .kicad_sch files, old on the left and new on the right, like a side-by-side code diff. It sits under the drawing on both tabs.

It's off by default because it makes pages bigger:

kigit --source HEAD~1..HEAD

or tick Include source in the GUI.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Removed lines are red, added lines green, and the changed part of a line is marked. Long unchanged stretches are folded (click to unfold).

Hover The panel shows A trace, via or pad Its own change first, then every other changed item on its net (and the net's pours) A pad of a moved or edited footprint The footprint's change first A footprint in the sidebar list That footprint A wire, label or pin (schematic) The net's changed wires and labels, on every sheet A part Its symbol's text A bus Its changed segments and bus labels

Each change says where it is (owl_v1.kicad_pcb:722 → :722), so you can find it in an editor.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
• Click pins the target, so you can move into the panel and scroll.
  • Drag its top edge to resize it.
  • The Source button collapses it.

Info

Only changed items' text goes into the page, not whole files. A pour's text stops before KiCad's computed fill polygons.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Comparing two versions of a board takes three steps:

  1. Point kigit at a project: run it inside a KiCad project folder, give the folder with -C, or open it in the GUI.
  2. Pick two revisions: commits, branches, tags, HEAD~3, or LOCAL for your uncommitted changes.
  3. Read the page: kigit writes one HTML page and opens it in your browser, with the PCB and the schematic as tabs.
flowchart LR
    A[git history] -->|old revision| K(kigit)
    A -->|new revision| K
    K --> P[PCB diff]
    K --> S[Schematic diff]
    P --> H[viewer.html]
    S --> H

docs.title: Minimal setup
docs.text:
cd ~/boards/my-board
kigit                      # HEAD vs the working tree (your uncommitted changes)
kigit HEAD~3               # HEAD~3 vs the working tree
kigit c46da63..HEAD        # two commits

The page is written to .kigit/ next to the board (or wherever -o FILE says) and opened in your browser. The terminal also prints a summary of the most-changed nets and of the schematic changes.

docs.title: Which way to use it
docs.text: You want to... Use Browse the history and click two commits GUI Compare from a script, a hook or CI Command Line Compare two copies of a project without git Without Git

docs.title: Colours
docs.text:
The same colours are used everywhere:

Colour Meaning Green Added in the newer revision Red (dashed on the schematic) Removed Blue Moved (same item, new place) Amber Schematic part whose value, footprint or connections changed Grey Unchanged
